candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Rejecting normative vocabulary may reflect cognitive, emotional, or cultural closure to objectively available improvements in conscious experience.
candidates.attributionBasis: The position continues Harris's preceding concession and directly characterizes O'Connor and similar skeptics from the opposing perspective.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies a central reply to emotivism by arguing that resistance to moral language can conceal ignorance of attainable forms of well-being rather than expose an absence of moral facts.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's claim that preference improvement and instrumental science require no moral prescriptions or genuine judgments of ought.

candidates.contextSummary: After O'Connor's preference-changing pill example, Harris argues that people who avoid normative terms may simply be closed to better modes of life they have not yet encountered.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: The possibility of unknown, preferable experiences does not require belief in morality or introduce any genuinely normative property.
candidates.attributionBasis: The first-person skeptical response matches O'Connor's established emotivist position and immediately challenges Harris's preceding inference.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move blocks Harris's attempted bridge from undiscovered improvements in experience to morality by preserving a wholly preference-based interpretation of those improvements.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's suggestion that ignorance of better attainable experiences undermines the skeptic's attempt to dispense with moral shoulds and oughts.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor accepts that he may be unaware of experiences he would prefer while denying that this epistemic possibility supplies any concept of morality.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Even while bracketing moral judgment, experiences occupy a descriptively value-laden landscape in which some states feel substantially better than others.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly brackets morality in order to restate Harris's descriptive well-being framework against O'Connor's objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This clarifies Harris's foundational route from facts about consciousness to value by locating evaluative differences within experience before applying explicitly moral terminology.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's contention that unknown preferable experiences remain entirely outside morality and therefore do not support objective moral truth.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris temporarily sets aside the judgmental force of moral language and emphasizes the factual experiential contrast between states worth seeking and states worth avoiding.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: Experiential value is subjective, while objective facts concern only which means most effectively realize a subject's existing values.
candidates.attributionBasis: The explicit statement of the speaker's own view tracks O'Connor's prior distinction between subjective preferences and instrumental scientific facts.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This states the con side's core reduction: science can objectively identify effective means, but the ends remain subjectively valued and do not become objective moral prescriptions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's characterization of experiential differences as a descriptively value-laden landscape capable of grounding further normative conclusions.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor accepts objective knowledge about conscious systems and effective action but confines value itself to the preferences of the experiencing subject.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Calling value an appearance in consciousness is not deflationary because conscious appearances have an irreducible ontological status that physical correlations do not eliminate.
candidates.attributionBasis: The immediate rebuttal rejects O'Connor's proposed deflation and develops Harris's characteristic argument about consciousness and irreducible appearances.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reply protects the pro grounding thesis from subjectivist reduction by arguing that experiential value remains real as consciousness even when it exists only phenomenally.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's distinction between merely subjective experiential value and objective facts about the instrumental means for satisfying it.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris argues that locating value within conscious appearance does not diminish its reality, since consciousness is known through experience and cannot simply be conceptually reduced away.

candidates.speaker: Alex O'Connor
candidates.proposition: A complete account of agents pursuing preferences, cooperating instrumentally, and discovering new pleasures can omit objective moral truth without explanatory loss.
candidates.attributionBasis: The extended first-person thought experiment reiterates O'Connor's preference-based framework and culminates in a direct challenge to objective morality.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the con side's principal explanatory-elimination argument: preference, cooperation, and empirical learning appear sufficient, leaving objective moral properties with no necessary role.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that the reality and irreducibility of conscious value prevents a preference-based account from deflating objective morality.

candidates.contextSummary: O'Connor constructs a stripped-down world in which agents scientifically pursue and expand their pleasures, then asks what is missing if no objective moral fact appears in that story.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Once the experiential possibilities are fully specified, navigation toward well-being supplies the right and wrong answers sought through moral language.
candidates.attributionBasis: The answer directly follows O'Connor's challenge and uses Harris's established navigation and well-being framework to identify objective practical answers.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly asserts the pro side's core identity claim: sufficiently complete facts about possible experience and well-being provide everything substantive meant by moral rightness and wrongness.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's desert-island account claiming that preference satisfaction and instrumental cooperation exhaust the facts while objective morality remains absent.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris answers that filling in the agents' possible experiences reveals genuine alternatives and objectively better or worse routes for maximizing their well-being.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Actions that cause immediate mutual suffering and foreclose future cooperation are objectively worse than alternatives that move conscious beings away from misery.
candidates.attributionBasis: The concrete two-person example continues Harris's answer and applies his well-being criterion to distinguish worse from better possibilities.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The example operationalizes the central grounding claim by showing how consequences for suffering, collaboration, and future experience yield non-arbitrary comparative answers.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: O'Connor's claim that the island agents' choices can be fully understood as preference satisfaction without any objective moral right or wrong.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris contrasts mutual violence with cooperative possibilities and grounds their objective difference in the lawful effects those choices have on conscious experience.
